subject: Music
practicalPaper: Practical musicianship is examined in Paper 3A, a 45-minute recorded aural test of seven compulsory items (rhythm, melody, two-part writing, chords, cadences, modulations and themes) for 50 marks, and Paper 3B, a 30-minute performance test on voice or an approved instrument (technical exercises and scales 10, a List A piece 15, a List B piece 15 and sight-reading 10) for 50 marks. Written practical skills such as harmonisation, melody continuation and setting a text are tested in the compulsory theory/composition question of Paper 2.

practicals.title: Rhythmic dictation on a monotone
practicals.aim: To write down, on a single line (monotone), the rhythm of a melody of not more than four bars played four times, in simple or compound time.
apparatus: Keyboard, piano or recorded playback (phone with speaker)
materials: Manuscript paper or a one-line rhythm stave
Practice recordings or a partner who plays short melodies
safety: Keep playback volume moderate to protect hearing, especially with earphones
Sit upright with good lighting to avoid eye and neck strain during long writing sessions
procedure: Note the time signature and the starting beat given on the answer sheet, and decide whether the beat is a crotchet (simple time) or a dotted crotchet (compound time).
First hearing: listen only, tapping the beat lightly on the desk and counting the number of bars; mark the bar lines on your line in advance.
Second hearing: write the long notes, rests and any obvious patterns (e.g. a dotted rhythm or a group of quavers) in the correct bars.
Third hearing: fill in the remaining rhythms, using rhythm syllables (e.g. ta, ta-te, ta-fa-te-fe) or counting to locate each note on the beat.
Fourth hearing: check every bar against the music, then count the beats in each bar to make sure the total matches the time signature.
Neaten the answer: correct stems, beams grouped by beat, rests placed clearly, and a final double bar line.
practicals.expectedObservations: A clean rhythm on one line with the correct number of bars, every bar adding up to the time signature, notes beamed by beats (in 6/8 quavers beamed in threes) and the final note held to the end of the last bar.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Checking the beats per bar. In 6/8 each bar holds 2 dotted-crotchet beats = 6 quavers, so a 4-bar exercise holds 4 x 6 = 24 quavers. Example bar: dotted crotchet (3 quavers) + crotchet (2) + quaver (1) = 6 quavers - correct. In 3/4 a 4-bar answer must total 4 x 3 = 12 crotchet beats; a bar written as minim (2) + crotchet (1) + quaver (0.5) = 3.5 beats is wrong and loses the mark for that bar. The test carries 8 marks, so roughly 2 marks per bar.
precautions: Write lightly on early hearings so corrections are easy
Mark bar lines before the second hearing
Count every bar before the final hearing ends
sourcesOfError: Losing the pulse when the melody has long notes or ties
Confusing a dotted rhythm with even quavers
Mishearing a rest as a held note
commonMistakes: Writing pitches on a full stave when only the rhythm is asked for
Beaming 6/8 quavers in twos as if it were 3/4
Bars that do not add up to the time signature
examTips: Marks are given bar by bar, so a correct bar earns marks even if another is wrong
Always finish with a double bar line and a full last bar
Use rhythm syllables silently to fix difficult beats

checkQuestions.q: How many quavers make up one bar of 6/8 time?
checkQuestions.explanation: 6/8 has six quaver beats grouped as two dotted crotchets.

checkQuestions.q: A 4-bar answer in 3/4 time should contain a total of how many crotchet beats?
checkQuestions.explanation: 4 bars x 3 crotchet beats = 12.

checkQuestions.q: In compound duple time the main beat is a
checkQuestions.explanation: Compound time divides each beat into three, so the beat is dotted.

practicals.title: Melody writing from dictation
practicals.aim: To write down on the stave a short melody of not more than four bars, in a major or minor key or a mode (including African-style melodies), after hearing it several times.
apparatus: Tuning fork or app sounding the tonic
safety: Moderate playback volume
Take short rests between exercises to avoid listening fatigue
procedure: Read the key signature, time signature and the given first note; sing the tonic chord (doh-me-soh) quietly to fix the key.
First hearing: listen and sing the melody back in your head in solfa; note whether it moves by step or leap and where it ends (usually doh).
Second hearing: write the rhythm above the stave for each bar.
Third hearing: write the solfa names under the rhythm, then convert them to stave notes in the given key.
Fourth hearing: check leaps (especially soh-doh and me-soh), accidentals (e.g. the raised 7th, se, in a minor key) and the final note.
Copy the final version neatly with correct stems, clef and bar lines.
practicals.expectedObservations: A melody in the correct key, starting on the given note, with mostly stepwise motion and typical leaps within the tonic chord, ending on the tonic, rhythmically complete in every bar.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Converting solfa to pitch in G major (doh = G): d r m f s l t d' = G A B C D E F# G. A heard pattern s-m-r-d from the D above the tonic gives D-B-A-G. Interval check: G up to D is a perfect 5th = 7 semitones (G-G#-A-A#-B-C-C#-D). In A minor the raised 7th (se) is G#, which is 1 semitone below the tonic A. This test carries 8 marks: 4 bars x 2 marks, each bar marked for pitch and rhythm.
precautions: Fix the key by singing the tonic chord first
Write rhythm and pitch as separate passes
Check accidentals needed in minor keys
sourcesOfError: Losing the tonal centre after a leap
Hearing the leading note as the tonic
Mixing up a 3rd and a 4th leap
commonMistakes: Ignoring the key signature when converting solfa
Forgetting the raised 7th in harmonic minor
Ending on a note other than the one heard
examTips: Most dictation melodies end on doh - use this to check
Write solfa first, staff notation last
Pitch and rhythm are both marked, so a correct rhythm still scores

checkQuestions.q: In G major, what note is "te"?
checkQuestions.explanation: G major has one sharp, F#, which is the 7th degree (te).

checkQuestions.q: How many semitones are in a perfect 5th?
checkQuestions.explanation: A perfect 5th spans 7 semitones, e.g. C to G.

checkQuestions.q: In A harmonic minor, which note is raised?
checkQuestions.explanation: The 7th degree G becomes G# to form a leading note.

practicals.title: Writing the missing part of a two-part phrase
practicals.aim: To hear a two-part phrase of not more than four bars and write the missing upper or lower part when the other part is printed.
apparatus: Two singers or two instruments for class practice
materials: Manuscript paper with the given part
safety: Moderate volume; rest the ears between hearings
procedure: Study the printed part: key, time, range and the cadence at the end.
First hearing: follow the printed part with your eye and listen for the other part; decide whether it moves in parallel 3rds/6ths, contrary motion or holds notes.
Second hearing: write the rhythm of the missing part (it often differs from the given part).
Third hearing: write the pitches, using the given part as a reference: measure each vertical interval (3rd, 6th, octave).
Fourth hearing: check the cadence; the bass usually ends s-d (perfect) or the upper part ends on doh or me.
Check that no note of your part crosses or clashes with the given part unless it was heard.
practicals.expectedObservations: The missing part fits the given part mostly in 3rds, 6ths and octaves, with contrary motion at cadences and a clear final cadence.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Using intervals from the given part. Given upper part in C major: E-F-G-E; the lower part heard a 3rd below each note gives C-D-E-C (E down 4 semitones = C, a major 3rd; F down 3 semitones = D, a minor 3rd). A 6th below E is G (E to G below = 9 semitones, a major 6th). Mark weighting: 8 marks over 4 bars = 2 marks per bar.
precautions: Use the printed part as your tuning reference
Write the rhythm before pitches
Check vertical intervals at each beat
sourcesOfError: Confusing which part is moving
Mishearing a 3rd as a 6th because of inversion
commonMistakes: Copying the rhythm of the given part when the missing part is different
Writing parallel 5ths or octaves that were not heard
examTips: Thirds and sixths are the commonest intervals between parts
Cadences are almost always standard - use theory to predict them

checkQuestions.q: How many semitones are in a major 3rd?
checkQuestions.explanation: A major 3rd = 4 semitones, e.g. C-E.

checkQuestions.q: The inversion of a 3rd is a
checkQuestions.explanation: Interval + inversion = 9, so 3rd inverts to 6th.

checkQuestions.q: Two parts moving in opposite directions are in
checkQuestions.explanation: Contrary motion means one part rises while the other falls.

practicals.title: Identifying chords in a progression
practicals.aim: To identify up to eight chords in a progression in a named key, using Roman numerals (I, ii, IV, V, V7, vi, Ic) or technical names.
materials: Answer grid with boxes for each chord
safety: Moderate volume
procedure: Play or sing the tonic chord of the named key to establish it.
First hearing: concentrate on the bass line only and write it in solfa (d, f, s, l...).
Second hearing: link each bass note to its likely chord: d = I, f = IV (or ii7), s = V, l = vi, r = ii; a bass on soh before V-I suggests Ic.
Third hearing: listen for the quality: major chords (I, IV, V) sound bright; minor chords (ii, vi) darker; V7 has a clash wanting to resolve.
Final hearing: check that the last two chords form a sensible cadence.
practicals.expectedObservations: A list such as I - IV - Ic - V - I with chords that follow normal progression habits and end with a cadence.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Chords in G major: I = G-B-D; ii = A-C-E; IV = C-E-G; V = D-F#-A; V7 = D-F#-A-C; vi = E-G-B. A heard bass of G-C-D-D-G with the 4th chord containing a C clashing against the D gives I - IV - V - V7 - I. Marks: 8 marks for up to 8 chords, so each chord is worth 1 mark.
precautions: Identify the bass first
Use the key given; do not change key unless instructed
Use standard Roman numeral symbols
sourcesOfError: Confusing IV and ii (they share two notes)
Missing a second inversion (Ic) because its bass is soh
commonMistakes: Writing letter names instead of Roman numerals when numerals are asked for
Calling V7 simply V
examTips: The chord before the final tonic is very often V or V7
A bass on soh followed by soh again often signals Ic-V

checkQuestions.q: What are the notes of chord V in G major?
checkQuestions.explanation: The dominant of G is D; the triad is D-F#-A.

checkQuestions.q: Which chord is minor in a major key?
checkQuestions.explanation: ii, iii and vi are minor in a major key.

checkQuestions.q: A chord with the 5th in the bass is in
checkQuestions.explanation: Second inversion (c) has the 5th in the bass.

practicals.title: Recognising cadences by ear
practicals.aim: To recognise and name perfect, imperfect, interrupted and plagal cadences in a major key.
safety: Moderate volume
procedure: Play the four cadences in C major slowly at the keyboard: V-I (G-C), IV-I (F-C), V-vi (G-Am), I-V (C-G).
Describe the feel of each: perfect = final and complete; plagal = soft "Amen"; interrupted = surprise; imperfect = unfinished, like a comma.
Listen to each exam example and focus on the last two chords and the bass movement (s-d perfect, f-d plagal, s-l interrupted, ends on s imperfect).
Write the name of each cadence clearly in full.
Practise with familiar hymns and Nigerian choral pieces, naming the cadence at the end of each line.
practicals.expectedObservations: Perfect cadences end strongly on the tonic; plagal cadences sound gentle; interrupted cadences move to the minor chord vi; imperfect cadences end on the dominant and sound unfinished.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Bass movement in C major: perfect G-C (falls a perfect 5th = 7 semitones, or rises a 4th = 5 semitones); plagal F-C (falls a perfect 4th = 5 semitones); interrupted G-A (rises a tone = 2 semitones); imperfect ends on G. Marking: 4 examples worth 6 marks in total = 1.5 marks each.
precautions: Focus only on the final two chords
Write the full name, not an abbreviation
sourcesOfError: Mistaking plagal for perfect because both end on I
Not noticing the minor chord in an interrupted cadence
commonMistakes: Naming a phrase ending on V as perfect
Spelling errors such as "plagel"
examTips: Ask: does it end on the tonic? If not, it is imperfect or interrupted
Listen to the bass - it decides most cadences

checkQuestions.q: Which progression forms a plagal cadence?
checkQuestions.explanation: Plagal is IV-I, the "Amen" cadence.

checkQuestions.q: A cadence ending on chord vi after V is
checkQuestions.explanation: V-vi is the interrupted (deceptive) cadence.

checkQuestions.q: Which cadence sounds unfinished, like a comma?
checkQuestions.explanation: The imperfect cadence ends on V.

practicals.title: Recognising modulations to related keys
practicals.aim: To recognise by ear and on paper a change of key from the tonic to the dominant, subdominant, relative minor or relative major.
safety: Moderate volume
procedure: Work out the related keys of the home key on paper (e.g. from C major: G major, F major, A minor).
Play a short passage in C that cadences in each related key and note the new accidental: F# (G major), B flat (F major), G# (A minor).
In each test example, sing the opening tonic and then sing the final note; compare its position (soh, fah or lah of the old key).
Listen for the bright lift of a dominant modulation, the relaxed fall of a subdominant one, and the darker colour of the relative minor.
Write the name of the new key relationship (e.g. "dominant") as instructed.
practicals.expectedObservations: Each passage ends with a perfect cadence in the new key; the final note corresponds to soh (dominant), fah (subdominant) or lah (relative minor) of the original key.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: From C major: dominant = G major (adds F#, the new key is 7 semitones above); subdominant = F major (adds B flat, 5 semitones above); relative minor = A minor (shares the key signature; harmonic form adds G#; tonic 3 semitones below C). From D major (2 sharps): dominant A major has 3 sharps, subdominant G major has 1 sharp, relative minor B minor uses A#. Marking: 4 examples for 6 marks = 1.5 marks each.
precautions: Keep the original tonic in mind throughout
Listen for new accidentals
sourcesOfError: Losing the home key in long passages
Confusing subdominant with relative minor
commonMistakes: Naming the new key letter instead of the relationship asked for (or the reverse)
Forgetting that the relative minor keeps the same key signature
examTips: Dominant modulation usually brings a sharpened fah (fe)
Subdominant modulation brings a flattened te (ta)
Relative minor brings sharpened soh (se)

checkQuestions.q: The dominant key of D major is
checkQuestions.explanation: The 5th degree of D is A.

checkQuestions.q: Which accidental typically appears when modulating from C major to A minor?
checkQuestions.explanation: The raised 7th of A minor is G#.

checkQuestions.q: The subdominant key of C major is
checkQuestions.explanation: F is the 4th degree of C.

practicals.title: Identifying and describing themes and excerpts
practicals.aim: To describe recorded excerpts (at least one African) by form, style or genre, principal instruments, scale or mode, and metre.
apparatus: Recordings: highlife, juju, Afrobeat, a Baroque concerto, a Classical symphony, a choral anthem
materials: Listening chart with headings: genre, instruments, scale/mode, metre, texture
safety: Moderate volume; avoid earphones at high level
procedure: Prepare a listening chart with the five headings.
First hearing: tap the beat and decide whether it is in 2, 3 or 4 and whether simple or compound.
Second hearing: name the main instruments (e.g. talking drum, agidigbo, guitars, horns, strings, harpsichord).
Third hearing: decide the scale or mode (major, minor, pentatonic) and texture (call and response, homophonic, polyphonic).
Name the genre or style and justify it with two features heard.
Compare your notes with a classmate and play the excerpt again to settle disagreements.
practicals.expectedObservations: For example, a juju excerpt shows talking drum, electric guitars, call-and-response vocals in Yoruba, duple metre and a major/pentatonic melody; a Baroque concerto shows harpsichord continuo, strings, a solo instrument and steady motor rhythm.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Estimating metre from beat counting: if you count 24 beats in 12 seconds the tempo is 24 / 12 x 60 = 120 beats per minute; accents every 2 beats give duple metre, so 12 seconds contains 12 bars of 2. Marking: 3 excerpts for 6 marks = 2 marks each, usually one mark per correct feature.
precautions: Write only what you hear, not what you expect
Use correct instrument names
sourcesOfError: Confusing similar Nigerian genres (juju and fuji)
Mistaking compound duple for triple metre
commonMistakes: Giving vague answers such as "drums" instead of "talking drum (dundun)"
Describing feelings instead of musical features
examTips: Name specific instruments and the genre with a reason
Fuji is percussion-and-voice based; juju features guitars and talking drum

checkQuestions.q: Call and response between a leader and chorus is an example of
checkQuestions.explanation: Antiphony alternates groups or leader and chorus.

checkQuestions.q: If 30 beats are counted in 15 seconds, the tempo is
A harpsichord playing continuo is typical of which period?
checkQuestions.explanation: Basso continuo is a hallmark of Baroque music.

practicals.title: Technical exercises: scales and arpeggios
practicals.aim: To play or sing the required major and minor scales and arpeggios accurately, evenly and with correct fingering or breathing for the performance test.
apparatus: Chosen instrument (keyboard, recorder, atenteben, guitar, trumpet etc.) or voice
safety: Warm up hands or voice for 5 minutes before playing
Sit or stand with relaxed shoulders to prevent strain
Clean wind instrument mouthpieces; do not share without cleaning
procedure: Warm up with slow long notes (wind/voice) or five-finger exercises (keyboard).
Play each scale hands separately (keyboard) or slowly, checking fingering (e.g. right hand C major 1-2-3-1-2-3-4-5).
Set the metronome at a comfortable speed (e.g. crotchet = 60, two notes per beat) and play the scale evenly up and down.
Raise the speed by 4-6 bpm only when three clean runs are achieved.
Play the matching arpeggio (doh-me-soh-doh') ascending and descending.
Record yourself and check evenness, tone and accuracy of the top and bottom notes.
practicals.expectedObservations: Even notes, no hesitation at the thumb crossing or register change, clear tone, correct accidentals in minor scales and a confident return to the tonic.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A two-octave scale played up and down contains 15 notes ascending and 14 more descending = 29 notes. At crotchet = 80 with two notes per beat (quavers), 29 notes take about 29 / 2 = 14.5 beats = 14.5 x 60 / 80 = 10.9 seconds. Mark weighting in Paper 3B: technical exercises/scales 10 of the 50 marks = 20%.
precautions: Practise slowly before fast
Use the same fingering every time
Listen to tuning on wind and string instruments
sourcesOfError: Rushing at the top of the scale
Uneven thumb crossings
Poor breath support on high notes
commonMistakes: Wrong accidentals in melodic minor descending (should revert to natural minor)
Stopping and restarting during the exam
examTips: Keep going after a slip - continuity is marked
Choose a steady tempo you can control
Announce or know the key requested before starting

checkQuestions.q: How many notes are played in a two-octave scale ascending and descending?
checkQuestions.explanation: 15 up, 14 down (top note shared) = 29.

checkQuestions.q: The melodic minor scale descending is the same as the
checkQuestions.explanation: Melodic minor raises 6 and 7 ascending only.

checkQuestions.q: What fraction of the Paper 3B marks is given to technical exercises and scales?
checkQuestions.explanation: 10 of 50 marks = 1/5.

practicals.title: Preparing and performing List A and List B pieces
practicals.aim: To prepare two contrasting pieces from the approved lists and perform them accurately, musically and with good tone before an examiner.
materials: Pencil for marking breaths, fingering and dynamics
safety: Take breaks every 25-30 minutes to avoid repetitive strain
Hydrate and avoid shouting before singing exams
procedure: Choose one List A and one List B piece that suit your range and technique; check they are on the current approved list.
Study each score: key, time, tempo marks, dynamics, articulation and form (e.g. ternary).
Learn difficult passages slowly in short sections, then join them.
Mark breaths, fingering and phrasing in pencil; practise with a metronome, then without.
Perform the whole piece daily to a friend or family member and record it.
Do a mock exam: walk in, tune, announce the pieces and play straight through without stopping.
practicals.expectedObservations: Secure notes and rhythm, steady tempo, audible dynamic contrast, phrasing that shapes the melody and confident stage presence.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Practice planning: a 64-bar piece in 4/4 at crotchet = 96 lasts 64 x 4 x 60 / 96 = 160 seconds (2 min 40 s). If you practise 4 sections of 16 bars for 15 minutes each, that is 60 minutes daily. Marks: List A 15 + List B 15 = 30 of the 50 performance marks (60%).
precautions: Keep the pulse steady; do not speed up in easy passages
Tune before playing
Observe all dynamics and repeats as directed
sourcesOfError: Nervousness affecting breath and tempo
Unfamiliar exam room acoustics
commonMistakes: Choosing a piece above your level
Ignoring dynamics
Stopping to correct mistakes
examTips: Examiners reward musical expression, not just correct notes
Recover quickly from slips
Bring a clean copy of the music

checkQuestions.q: How long does a 64-bar piece in 4/4 at crotchet = 96 last?
checkQuestions.explanation: 64 x 4 = 256 beats; 256 / 96 min = 2.67 min = 2 min 40 s.

checkQuestions.q: Together the two prepared pieces carry how many marks?
What should a candidate do after a small slip?
checkQuestions.explanation: Continuity is rewarded; keep the pulse going.

practicals.title: Sight-reading tests
practicals.aim: To read and perform an unseen short passage in simple or compound time with correct pitch, rhythm and pulse.
safety: Keep a relaxed posture
procedure: Use the inspection time (about 30 seconds) to note key signature, time signature, accidentals and tempo marking.
Identify patterns: scale passages, arpeggios, repeated rhythms.
Tap or clap the rhythm silently while counting the beats.
Choose a slow, steady tempo and count one bar in.
Perform without stopping, keeping the pulse even if a note is wrong.
Practise daily with a new exercise, increasing difficulty gradually.
practicals.expectedObservations: A continuous, steady performance with mostly correct notes and rhythms and observed dynamics.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Inspection planning: with 30 seconds for an 8-bar exercise you have about 30 / 8 = 3.75 seconds per bar. A passage in 6/8 at dotted crotchet = 60 lasts 8 bars x 2 beats x 1 s = 16 seconds. Sight reading carries 10 of 50 marks (two tests, about 5 marks each).
precautions: Never stop to correct
Read ahead by at least one bar
sourcesOfError: Missing an accidental in the key signature
Starting too fast
commonMistakes: Ignoring the time signature
Looking at the hands instead of the music
examTips: A steady pulse earns more marks than correct notes with stops
Check the key signature twice

checkQuestions.q: What is the best thing to do in the inspection time?
checkQuestions.explanation: Study key, time, accidentals and patterns.

checkQuestions.q: How long do 8 bars of 6/8 at dotted crotchet = 60 last?
checkQuestions.explanation: 2 beats per bar x 8 = 16 beats at 1 per second.

checkQuestions.q: Which quality is most important in sight-reading?
checkQuestions.explanation: Continuity and pulse are rewarded most.

practicals.title: Transcribing staff notation into tonic solfa and back
practicals.aim: To transcribe a melody accurately from staff notation into tonic solfa (with rhythm signs) and from solfa into staff notation.
materials: A short hymn or Nigerian folk song in both notations
safety: Good lighting and posture when writing
procedure: Identify the key from the key signature and find doh (e.g. two sharps: D major, doh = D).
Write the solfa key statement (e.g. Doh is D) and the time signature.
Name each note in solfa, adding octave marks: d' for upper and d, for lower octave.
Add solfa rhythm signs: bar line |, beat divider :, half-beat . and continuation dash -.
For solfa to staff, reverse the process: place doh on the stave, then each note, and convert the rhythm signs to note values.
Play both versions to check they sound the same.
practicals.expectedObservations: Both versions agree in pitch and rhythm; each bar contains the correct number of beats.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Key D major, 4/4. Staff bar: D(crotchet) F#(crotchet) A(minim) becomes | d : m : s : - |. In D major: D=d, E=r, F#=m, G=f, A=s, B=l, C#=t. Beat check: 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 beats. For a 2/4 bar with two quavers then a crotchet the solfa is | s .f : m | (half-beat dot between s and f).
precautions: State the key (Doh is ...) at the start
Mark octave changes
Keep beats aligned
sourcesOfError: Wrong doh from misreading the key signature
Missing octave marks
commonMistakes: Writing letter names instead of solfa
Using the wrong rhythm sign for half beats
examTips: Marks are lost bar by bar for rhythm errors, so check beats
Always include the key statement

checkQuestions.q: In D major, which note is "me"?
checkQuestions.explanation: D-E-F#: the 3rd degree is F#.

checkQuestions.q: In solfa notation a colon ( : ) separates
checkQuestions.explanation: The colon divides beats within a bar.

checkQuestions.q: A key signature of three flats in a major key gives doh =
checkQuestions.explanation: Three flats is E flat major.

practicals.title: Transposing a melody and writing for transposing instruments
practicals.aim: To transpose a melody into another key and write the correct part for a B flat instrument (clarinet, trumpet) from concert pitch.
safety: Good posture and lighting while writing
procedure: Identify the original key and the interval of transposition (a B flat instrument sounds a major 2nd lower than written, so write a major 2nd higher).
Write the new key signature first (e.g. concert E flat major becomes written F major).
Move every note by the same interval, keeping the same letter-name step (a major 2nd is always the next letter up).
Adjust accidentals: a raised note stays raised relative to the new key.
Copy the rhythm, dynamics and slurs unchanged.
Play both versions to check the intervals between notes are unchanged.
practicals.expectedObservations: The melody shape and rhythm are identical; only the key and pitch level change; written notes for a B flat instrument are a tone higher than concert pitch.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Concert E flat major (3 flats) up a major 2nd (2 semitones) = F major (1 flat). Concert notes E flat - G - B flat - A flat become written F - A - C - B flat. Check: E flat to F = 2 semitones; G to A = 2 semitones; B flat to C = 2 semitones. Each pair keeps the same interval: E flat to G is a major 3rd (4 semitones) and F to A is also 4 semitones.
precautions: Change the key signature before moving notes
Keep the letter-name step consistent
Watch accidentals
sourcesOfError: Using the wrong direction for transposing instruments
Miscounting semitones
commonMistakes: Forgetting the new key signature
Transposing a 2nd by letter but not checking tone vs semitone
examTips: Show the new key signature clearly - it carries marks
B flat instruments: write a major 2nd higher; F horn: write a perfect 5th higher

checkQuestions.q: A B flat clarinet must read music written
options: a major 2nd higher than concert pitch
checkQuestions.explanation: It sounds a major 2nd below written pitch.

checkQuestions.q: Concert E flat major is written for B flat trumpet in
checkQuestions.explanation: E flat up a major 2nd = F.

checkQuestions.q: How many semitones are in a major 2nd?
checkQuestions.explanation: A major 2nd = a whole tone = 2 semitones.

practicals.title: Naming and singing intervals
practicals.aim: To name intervals by number and quality on the stave and recognise them by ear.
safety: Moderate playing volume
procedure: Count the letter names from the lower to the upper note, including both, to get the number (C to E = 3rd).
Count semitones on the keyboard to get the quality.
Compare with the major scale of the lower note: if the upper note is in that scale the interval is major (2, 3, 6, 7) or perfect (4, 5, 8).
Apply alterations: one semitone smaller than major = minor; larger than perfect/major = augmented; smaller than minor/perfect = diminished.
Sing each interval using a familiar song opening to train the ear.
practicals.expectedObservations: Correct names such as major 3rd, perfect 5th, minor 6th, augmented 4th.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Semitone counts: minor 2nd 1, major 2nd 2, minor 3rd 3, major 3rd 4, perfect 4th 5, augmented 4th 6, perfect 5th 7, minor 6th 8, major 6th 9, minor 7th 10, major 7th 11, octave 12. Example: F up to B = 4th by letter (F G A B) and 6 semitones = augmented 4th. Inversion: a major 3rd (4) inverts to a minor 6th (12 - 4 = 8).
precautions: Count letters including both notes
Check the key signature for accidentals
sourcesOfError: Counting semitones incorrectly across E-F and B-C
commonMistakes: Calling F-B a perfect 4th
Forgetting accidentals from the key signature
examTips: Number first, quality second
Major inverts to minor, augmented to diminished, perfect stays perfect

checkQuestions.q: F up to B natural is a
checkQuestions.explanation: Six semitones over four letters = augmented 4th.

checkQuestions.q: A major 3rd inverts to a
checkQuestions.explanation: Major becomes minor; 3 + 6 = 9.

checkQuestions.q: How many semitones are in a minor 7th?
checkQuestions.explanation: Minor 7th = 10 semitones.

practicals.title: Harmonising a melody in four parts (SATB)
practicals.aim: To add alto, tenor and bass parts to a given soprano melody using primary and secondary triads, correct cadences and good voice-leading.
materials: Manuscript paper (two staves: treble and bass)
safety: Good posture and lighting while writing
procedure: Identify the key and the phrase endings; choose the cadences first (e.g. imperfect at bar 4, perfect at bar 8).
For each melody note list the chords that contain it (e.g. in C, the note G belongs to I, iii and V).
Choose a strong bass line moving mostly by step or by 4ths/5ths, with root-position chords at cadences.
Fill in alto and tenor, keeping each part within range (S C4-G5, A G3-D5, T C3-G4, B E2-C4) and spacing no more than an octave between S-A and A-T.
Double the root in root position; avoid doubling the leading note.
Check for consecutive 5ths and octaves and resolve the leading note upward to the tonic.
practicals.expectedObservations: A smooth four-part texture with logical chord choices, correct doubling, no parallel 5ths/octaves and clear cadences.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Example perfect cadence in C major: chord V (bass G2, tenor D4, alto G4, soprano B4) moves to chord I (bass C3, tenor E4, alto G4, soprano C5). Checks: the leading note B4 rises 1 semitone to C5; the bass G2 to C3 rises a perfect 4th (5 semitones); the alto keeps the common note G4; the tenor rises a tone (D4 to E4) so chord I contains its 3rd (E). Spacing: soprano C5 to alto G4 = 5 semitones and alto G4 to tenor E4 = 3 semitones, both within an octave (12). A typical teacher marking guide: chords 6, voice-leading 6, cadences 4, presentation 4 = 20 marks.
precautions: Write cadences first
Keep alto and tenor movements small
Check every pair of parts for parallels
sourcesOfError: Overlooking hidden consecutives between outer parts
Parts crossing
commonMistakes: Doubling the leading note
Using second inversion chords freely instead of only cadential or passing
Parts out of range
examTips: A neat, correct cadence earns marks even if earlier chords are weak
Label chords with Roman numerals if asked

checkQuestions.q: Which note should normally be doubled in a root-position major triad?
checkQuestions.explanation: Doubling the root is safest and strongest.

checkQuestions.q: Which consecutive intervals are forbidden between two parts in strict harmony?
checkQuestions.explanation: Parallel perfect 5ths and octaves weaken part independence.

checkQuestions.q: The leading note in chord V should usually move to
checkQuestions.explanation: Te rises to doh.

practicals.title: Continuing a given melodic phrase
practicals.aim: To continue a given opening to form a balanced melody of 12-16 bars, modulating to a specified related key where required, with tempo and dynamic marks.
apparatus: Keyboard or recorder for testing ideas
safety: Good posture and lighting
procedure: Study the opening: key, metre, range, rhythmic motif.
Plan the structure: e.g. 16 bars = A (4) A' (4) B (4, modulating to the dominant) A'' (4, returning to tonic).
Mark the cadence points: imperfect bar 4, perfect in the dominant bar 12, perfect in the tonic bar 16.
Develop the given motif using repetition, sequence and inversion; balance steps and leaps.
Introduce the new accidental for the modulation (e.g. fe = F# for G major from C).
Add tempo, dynamics and phrase marks; play it through and correct awkward leaps.
practicals.expectedObservations: A singable melody within about an octave and a half, built from the opening motif, with clear phrases, a modulation and a final perfect cadence on the tonic.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Structure: 4 phrases x 4 bars = 16 bars (within the 12-16 limit). A 3-phrase plan of 4 bars each gives 12 bars. In 3/4, a 16-bar melody contains 16 x 3 = 48 crotchet beats. Modulation from C major to G major adds F#; the cadence in G at bar 12 is D to G (melody often r'-d' in G, i.e. A to G).
precautions: Keep within the given length
Use the opening motif throughout
Return to the tonic at the end
sourcesOfError: Losing track of bar count
Forgetting accidentals after modulating
commonMistakes: Melodies that wander with no repeated ideas
Too many large leaps
No modulation when one is required
examTips: Examiners reward shape, unity and correct modulation
Add performance directions - they carry marks

checkQuestions.q: How many crotchet beats are in a 16-bar melody in 3/4?
Modulating from C major to its dominant introduces which note?
checkQuestions.explanation: G major has F#.

checkQuestions.q: Repeating a motif at a different pitch is called
checkQuestions.explanation: A sequence repeats a figure at a higher or lower pitch.

practicals.title: Setting an English text to music
practicals.aim: To set a short English text to an original melody with correct word stress, syllable placement and phrasing.
safety: Good posture and lighting
procedure: Read the text aloud several times and mark stressed syllables.
Count syllables in each line and decide the metre (e.g. stresses every other syllable suggest 2/4 or 4/4).
Place stressed syllables on strong beats (beat 1 or 3 in 4/4).
Plan the phrase structure to match the lines, with cadences at line endings.
Compose the melody, using slurs for syllables sung over more than one note.
Write the words under the notes with hyphens between syllables and extender lines for melismas.
practicals.expectedObservations: Strong syllables fall on strong beats; each line ends with a cadence; the melody reflects the mood of the words.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Line: "The rain falls soft upon the land" has 8 syllables (The-rain-falls-soft-up-on-the-land) with stresses on rain, soft, -on, land. In 4/4 with one crotchet per syllable and an upbeat on "The", the line fills 2 bars (8 beats) with "land" lengthened to a minim and an earlier beat shortened. Four such lines produce an 8-bar melody.
precautions: Match word stress to musical stress
Use hyphens and slurs correctly
sourcesOfError: Misreading word stress
Miscounting syllables
commonMistakes: Putting weak syllables such as "the" on the first beat
Words not aligned under notes
examTips: Write the words neatly under the notes - presentation is marked
Use an anacrusis (upbeat) for lines starting on a weak syllable

checkQuestions.q: A weak syllable that begins a line is best set as
checkQuestions.explanation: An upbeat lets the stressed syllable fall on beat 1.

checkQuestions.q: Singing one syllable over several notes is called
checkQuestions.explanation: A melisma spreads one syllable over several notes.

checkQuestions.q: How many syllables are in "upon the land"?
checkQuestions.explanation: Up-on-the-land = 4.

practicals.title: Identifying and classifying African musical instruments
practicals.aim: To identify, sketch and classify Nigerian traditional instruments into idiophones, membranophones, aerophones and chordophones and describe how they are played.
apparatus: Available instruments: dundun (talking drum), ekwe/slit drum, ogene (gong), shekere, udu, oja (flute), kakaki, goje, kora image
safety: Handle borrowed instruments gently and with permission
Do not blow wind instruments used by others without cleaning
procedure: Visit the school music room, a cultural centre or a local performer, or use a set of instruments in class.
For each instrument, record its local name, ethnic group, material and how sound is produced.
Sketch and label each instrument (e.g. hourglass body, tension cords and skins of the dundun).
Classify each by how the sound is made: the body itself (idiophone), a stretched skin (membranophone), air (aerophone) or strings (chordophone).
Note musical functions (rhythm, melody, signalling) and non-musical functions (royal announcement, ritual).
Present the findings in a table.
practicals.expectedObservations: Ogene, ekwe, shekere and udu are idiophones; dundun, bata and gangan are membranophones; oja and kakaki are aerophones; goje and kora are chordophones. The talking drum changes pitch when the cords are squeezed.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Classification tally from a class collection of 12 instruments: idiophones 5, membranophones 4, aerophones 2, chordophones 1 (total 12). Idiophones form 5 / 12 x 100 = 41.7% of the collection. Pitch: squeezing the dundun cords increases skin tension, raising pitch; a change from a low to a high tone may span about a 4th to a 5th (5-7 semitones).
precautions: Record local names with the ethnic group
Check classification by how sound is produced, not by material
sourcesOfError: Instruments with regional names that differ
Classifying a slit drum as a membranophone because it is called a drum
commonMistakes: Calling the ekwe a membranophone
Unlabelled sketches
examTips: Always state the sound-producing part to justify the class
Give a local example for each class

checkQuestions.q: The ekwe (slit drum) is classified as
checkQuestions.explanation: It has no skin; the wooden body vibrates.

checkQuestions.q: The dundun changes pitch because the player
checkQuestions.explanation: Squeezing tightens the skin and raises pitch.

checkQuestions.q: The goje is a
checkQuestions.explanation: It is a bowed string instrument.
